Review this SQL query for performance:
```sql
SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE YEAR(o.created_at) = 2025 AND o.customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%smith%') ORDER BY o.created_at;
```

steps.text:
### Quick performance‑impact checklist | Aspect | What the query does | Why it can be slow | Typical fix | |--------|--------------------|--------------------|-------------| | **`YEAR(o.created_at) = 2025`** | Extracts the year from the `created_at` timestamp for every row. | Wrapping the column in a function disables use of an index on `created_at`. The DB must evaluate the function on every row (full‑table scan or at least index‑scan of the whole table). | Write the predicate as a range on the raw column:
```sql
o.created_at >= '{{date:1}}' AND o.created_at < '{{date:2}}'
```
This lets the optimizer use an index on `created_at` (or a partition on the year). | | **Sub‑query `IN (SELECT id FROM customers …)`** | Finds all customers whose name contains “smith” (case‑insensitive depending on collation) and then filters orders by those IDs. | The sub‑query is executed once, but the `LIKE '%smith%'` pattern forces a full scan of `customers` because of the leading `%`. The resulting list may be large, leading to a large `IN` list. | Replace the `IN` with a **join** and push the `LIKE` predicate to the join side:
```sql
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '{{date:1}}' … AND c.name LIKE '%smith%'
```
If you can avoid the leading `%` (e.g., `smith%` or `'%smith'` after a full‑text index), you get an indexable search. | | **`LIKE '%smith%'`** | Looks for “smith” anywhere in the name. | The leading wildcard prevents use of a regular B‑tree index on `name`. The DB must scan every `customers` row. | • Create a **full‑text index** (or trigram/GIST index in PostgreSQL) and use `@@`/`MATCH … AGAINST`.
• If the pattern can be anchored (`smith%`), use a normal index. | | **`ORDER BY o.created_at`** | Sorts the result set by timestamp. | If the preceding predicates cannot use an index that already orders by `created_at`, the DB must materialize the rows and sort them (filesort), which adds I/O and CPU. | • Ensure the `created_at` range predicate is present (as above) and that there is an **index on (`created_at`, `customer_id`)** or a composite covering index that matches the join order.
• In MySQL, the optimizer can use “index‑scan” to return rows already sorted when the index order matches the `ORDER BY`. | | **`SELECT *`** | Returns every column from `orders`. | Pulls all columns even if you only need a few, increasing I/O and memory usage. | List only the columns you actually need, or create a **covering index** that includes those columns so the DB can satisfy the query from the index alone. | | **Potential data volume** | If the year 2025 has many orders and many customers contain “smith”, the result set could be huge. | Large result sets increase network traffic and client‑side processing time. | Add pagination (`LIMIT … OFFSET …`) or a tighter filter (e.g., status, region). | --- ### Revised version (MySQL / MariaDB style) ```sql -- Assuming we only need a few order columns, e.g. id, created_at, total_amount SELECT o.id, o.created_at, o.total_amount, c.name AS customer_name FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.created_at >= '2025-01-01' -- start of 2025 AND o.created_at < '2026-01-01' -- end of 2025 AND c.name LIKE '%smith%' -- consider full‑text index ORDER BY o.created_at; -- will be satisfied by an index on (created_at, customer_id) ``` **Index suggestions** ```sql -- 1. Index on orders.created_at (or a composite covering index) CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders (created_at); -- 2. Composite index that also covers the join column CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_customer ON orders (created_at, customer_id); -- 3. Full‑text index on customers.name (if using InnoDB full‑text) ALTER TABLE customers ADD FULLTEXT idx_customers_name (name); -- then replace LIKE with: MATCH(name) AGAINST('+smith' IN BOOLEAN MODE) ``` If you cannot change the schema, the most impactful change is the **date‑range predicate** (`created_at >= … AND < …`). That alone can turn a full scan into an indexed range scan, often cutting execution time dramatically. --- ### Bottom line | Change | Expected impact | |--------|-----------------| | Replace `YEAR(created_at) = 2025` with a date range | **High** – enables index use on `created_at`. | | Convert the `IN (SELECT …)` to a `JOIN` | **Medium** – lets the optimizer combine filters and may reduce temporary tables. | | Add a full‑text (or trigram) index for the `LIKE '%smith%'` search | **High** if the pattern stays with leading `%`. | | Add an index on `(created_at, customer_id)` (or at least on `created_at`) | **High** for both filtering and ordering. | | Select only needed columns | **Low‑Medium** – reduces I/O. | | Paginate or limit result set | **Low‑Medium** – reduces network load. | Apply the date‑range filter first (the cheapest change) and then evaluate the need for a full‑text index on `customers.name`. After those are in place, re‑run the query and examine the execution plan (`EXPLAIN`) to verify that the indexes are being used and that the sort is “Using filesort: No”.
